title: Why does putting a load balancer in front of app instances break things when a server stores LOCAL state (a session in App A's memory is invisible when the next request lands on App B) — how do you fix it (externalize session/state to a shared store like Redis, or go fully stateless with JWTs), why does round-robin NOT guarantee equal WORK (a 5ms request vs a multi-second one), and why must health checks verify the instance can actually SERVE (dependency/connection-pool healthy) rather than merely be running?
shortTitle: Why does a load balancer break things when a server stores local state, why doesn't round robin guarantee equal work, and why must health checks verify the instance can actually serve?

s1_definition.profdef: When a load balancer spreads requests across multiple app instances, any state stored in one instance's local memory becomes invisible to the others, so a session created on instance A is lost when the next request lands on instance B. The fix is to stop storing state locally: externalize it to a shared store like Redis, or go fully stateless with a self-contained token such as a JWT that carries the state in the request itself. Separately, round robin distributes the count of requests equally but not the amount of work, because a five-millisecond request and a multi-second request count the same, so equal request counts can produce very unequal load. Finally, health checks must verify that an instance can actually serve a request — its database connection pool and downstream dependencies are healthy — not merely that the process is running, because an instance can be up but unable to do any useful work.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has three identical counters and a floor manager sending customers to whichever is free. If teller A scribbles Rajesh's half-finished loan form on a sticky note on his own desk (local state), then Rajesh comes back and the manager sends him to teller B, teller B has never seen that note and Rajesh has to start over. The fix is to keep the form in a shared central filing cabinet (Redis) that any teller can open, or to have Rajesh carry a fully filled-out signed form with him every time (a JWT) so no teller needs to remember anything. Also, the manager sending the same number of customers to each counter is not fair if some customers take thirty seconds and others take an hour — equal headcount is not equal work. And the manager must check that a counter can actually serve — the teller has a working computer and an open vault line — not just that someone is sitting there, because a teller with a dead terminal is worse than an empty window.
s1_definition.oneliner: Local state breaks under a load balancer because requests scatter across instances, so externalize state to Redis or carry it in a JWT; round robin balances request count not work, so prefer least connections; and health checks must prove an instance can serve, not merely that it is alive.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When a load balancer spreads requests across multiple app instances, any state stored in one instance's local memory becomes invisible to the others, so a session created on instance A is lost when the next request lands on instance B. The fix is to stop storing state locally: externalize it to a shared store like Redis, or go fully stateless with a self-contained token such as a JWT that carries the state in the request itself. Separately, round robin distributes the count of requests equally but not the amount of work, because a five-millisecond request and a multi-second request count the same, so equal request counts can produce very unequal load. Finally, health checks must verify that an instance can actually serve a request — its database connection pool and downstream dependencies are healthy — not merely that the process is running, because an instance can be up but unable to do any useful work.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has three identical counters and a floor manager sending customers to whichever is free. If teller A scribbles Rajesh's half-finished loan form on a sticky note on his own desk (local state), then Rajesh comes back and the manager sends him to teller B, teller B has never seen that note and Rajesh has to start over. The fix is to keep the form in a shared central filing cabinet (Redis) that any teller can open, or to have Rajesh carry a fully filled-out signed form with him every time (a JWT) so no teller needs to remember anything. Also, the manager sending the same number of customers to each counter is not fair if some customers take thirty seconds and others take an hour — equal headcount is not equal work. And the manager must check that a counter can actually serve — the teller has a working computer and an open vault line — not just that someone is sitting there, because a teller with a dead terminal is worse than an empty window.

**One line to remember:** Local state breaks under a load balancer because requests scatter across instances, so externalize state to Redis or carry it in a JWT; round robin balances request count not work, so prefer least connections; and health checks must prove an instance can serve, not merely that it is alive.

sections.s2_technical:
The local-state problem comes directly from horizontal scaling behind a load balancer. With one instance, you could keep a user's session in that instance's memory and it was always there. The moment you run several instances and a load balancer distributes requests, consecutive requests from the same user may land on different instances. If instance A created an in-memory session and the next request goes to instance B, instance B has no idea the session exists, so the user appears logged out or their shopping cart is empty. This is the classic symptom of server-side local state in a multi-instance deployment.

There are two good fixes. The first is to externalize the state to a shared store that all instances can read and write, most commonly Redis for sessions. Now instance A writes the session to Redis and instance B reads it from Redis, so it does not matter which instance handles a request. A small example is replacing an in-memory map with `redis.set("session:" + id, json)` and `redis.get("session:" + id)`. The second fix is to go fully stateless using a self-contained token such as a JWT: the token carries the user's identity and claims, signed so it cannot be tampered with, and every request presents it, so no server needs to remember anything between requests. Stateless is the cleanest for scaling because any instance can serve any request with zero shared lookup. The weaker workaround is sticky sessions, pinning a user to one instance, but that undermines balancing and breaks when the instance dies, so it is a fallback, not the goal.

The round-robin fairness problem is about counting requests versus measuring work. Round robin guarantees each instance receives the same number of requests over time, but requests are not equal in cost. If instance A happens to receive several multi-second report generations while instance B receives several five-millisecond balance checks, both got the same count but A is overloaded and B is idle. Round robin is blind to this because it only tracks position, not load. The fix is a load-aware algorithm: least connections routes to the instance with the fewest in-flight requests, so an instance tied up with slow requests naturally receives fewer new ones, and least response time routes toward whoever is actually serving fastest. The lesson is that equal request distribution is not equal load distribution when request costs vary.

The health-check problem is about what "healthy" means. A naive health check (often called a liveness check) just confirms the process is running and the port is open. But an instance can be running yet unable to do any real work: its database connection pool may be exhausted or its downstream dependency may be unreachable, so every request it accepts will fail. If the load balancer only checks liveness, it keeps sending traffic to an instance that returns errors for everything, which is worse than removing it. The fix is a readiness health check that exercises the real ability to serve: it verifies the database connection pool can get a connection, critical downstream dependencies respond, and the instance is actually ready to handle requests. A small example is a `/health/ready` endpoint that does `dataSource.getConnection().isValid(1)` and pings critical dependencies, returning unhealthy if any fail, so the load balancer pulls the instance from rotation until it can truly serve.

The senior nuances tie these together. First, statelessness is the foundation of horizontal scaling; any local state is a scaling bug waiting to surface under a load balancer. Second, the choice of balancing algorithm must match request-cost variance, and most real systems should not assume uniform cost. Third, health checks should distinguish liveness (should the orchestrator restart this?) from readiness (should the load balancer send traffic?), because an instance that is temporarily unable to reach its database should be pulled from traffic without being killed. Fourth, a readiness check that is too strict can cascade: if a shared dependency blips and every instance reports unready at once, you can take down the whole service, so readiness checks need care and sometimes a degraded-but-serving state.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India scaled its API from one instance to three behind a load balancer and immediately hit three problems.

Problem 1 — Vanishing logins. Rajesh logged in, the session was stored in instance A's memory, and his next request landed on instance B, which did not know him, so he was bounced to the login screen repeatedly. This is the local-state problem. The fix is to store sessions in Redis (shared) or issue a JWT so any instance can serve any request.

Problem 2 — The lopsided load. Round robin sent equal request counts to all three instances, but the statement service mixed five-millisecond balance checks with multi-second thousand-page statements, so one instance got swamped while others idled. This is round robin balancing count not work. The fix is least connections.

Problem 3 — The zombie instance. Instance C's database connection pool was exhausted, so it failed every request, but the naive health check saw the process alive and kept routing to it. This is the health-check problem. The fix is a readiness check that verifies the pool and dependencies.

We will model a `LoadBalancer` with a session-aware flow. A `SessionStore` can be local (broken) or shared Redis-like (fixed). A `LeastConnections` strategy fixes the work imbalance. A readiness `HealthChecker` verifies each instance can truly serve. The demo shows the broken local-state case, the Redis fix, round robin versus least connections, and a zombie instance being pulled by readiness checks.

The code will have an `AppInstance` with a connection pool and a readiness check, a `SharedSessionStore`, a `LeastConnections` router, a `HealthChecker`, and a demo that reproduces and fixes all three problems.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three instances app-A, app-B, app-C; Rajesh (SAV2001) logs in; mixed fast and slow requests; app-C's pool is exhausted.

Step 1 — Rajesh logs in on app-A, which stores the session in its own memory. His next request is routed to app-B, which checks its local memory, finds nothing, and treats him as logged out. The local-state breakage is reproduced.

Step 2 — We apply the fix: the session is written to Redis. Now app-B reads the session from Redis and recognizes Rajesh. Because the state is shared, any instance can serve any request, which is the foundation of safe horizontal scaling. The alternative is a JWT carrying the identity so no store is needed at all.

Step 3 — Round robin had given each instance the same number of requests, but app-A happened to get two multi-second requests while app-B and app-C got five-millisecond ones. The load in milliseconds is wildly lopsided even though the counts were equal, proving round robin balances count, not work.

Step 4 — We switch to least connections. The next request is routed to the instance with the fewest active connections, steering away from the busy app-A, so work is actually balanced.

Step 5 — app-C's database connection pool is exhausted. A naive liveness check sees the process alive and would keep routing to it. The readiness check instead tries to get a database connection, fails, and reports app-C not ready, so the load balancer removes it from rotation. The following request is routed only among the instances that can actually serve.

Step 6 — The three fixes together — externalized state, load-aware balancing, and readiness checks — make the multi-instance deployment behave correctly.

```
       │
       ▼
  traffic flows only to instances that can ACTUALLY SERVE
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Putting a load balancer in front of multiple app instances exposes any local state as a bug. With one instance you could keep a session in its memory and it was always there, but once a load balancer spreads requests, consecutive requests from the same user can land on different instances, so a session created on instance A is invisible when the next request hits instance B, and the user appears logged out. The fix is to stop storing state locally: either externalize it to a shared store like Redis so instance A writes it and instance B reads it, or go fully stateless with a signed self-contained token such as a JWT that carries the identity in every request so no server needs to remember anything. Sticky sessions that pin a user to one instance are only a fallback because they undermine balancing and break when that instance dies.

Round robin does not guarantee equal work because it balances the count of requests, not their cost. If one instance happens to receive several multi-second report generations while another receives five-millisecond balance checks, both got the same number of requests but the first is overloaded and the second is idle. Round robin is blind to this because it only tracks position. The fix is a load-aware algorithm such as least connections, which routes to the instance with the fewest in-flight requests, so an instance tied up with slow work naturally receives fewer new requests, or least response time, which routes toward whoever is serving fastest.

Health checks must verify that an instance can actually serve, not merely that it is running. A naive liveness check confirms the process is up and the port is open, but an instance can be up yet unable to do real work because its database connection pool is exhausted or a downstream dependency is unreachable, so it fails every request it accepts, which is worse than being removed. The fix is a readiness check that exercises the real ability to serve, verifying the connection pool can hand out a connection and critical dependencies respond, so the load balancer pulls that instance from rotation until it can truly serve. In my banking platform I separated the readiness probe, which controls whether the load balancer sends traffic, from the liveness probe, which controls whether the orchestrator restarts the pod, so a pod that temporarily cannot reach its database is pulled from traffic without being killed.

The deeper principle is that statelessness is the foundation of horizontal scaling, that balancing must account for request-cost variance rather than assuming uniform cost, and that health must mean can-serve, not merely alive.

The one-line summary I give is: externalize state to Redis or carry it in a JWT so requests can scatter safely, use least connections because round robin balances count not work, and make health checks prove an instance can actually serve by testing its connection pool and dependencies, not just that the process is alive.
